1.pericope_label: And the Spirit of God came upon Azariah the son of Oded: And he went out to meet Asa, and said unto him, Hear ye me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin; The Lord is with you, while ye be with him; and if ye seek him, he will be found of you; but if ye forsake him, he will forsake you. Now for a long season Israel hath been without the true God, and without a teaching priest, and without law. But when they in their trouble did turn unto the Lord God of Israel, and sought him, he was found of them. And in those times there was no peace to him that went out, nor to him that came in, but great vexations were upon all the inhabitants of the countries. And nation was destroyed of nation, and city of city: for God did vex them with all adversity. Be ye strong therefore, and let not your hands be weak: for your work shall be rewarded.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the description as past and illustrative, periods of religious decline such as those recorded in the Book of Judges as well as later ones, adduced as historical proof that the Lord was with Israel while they were with him; he notes that the promise generalises the statement before it, that it is a favourite formula with the chronicler, and that the verbs are better rendered present than future. On the closing exhortation he supplies the moral, that the ruinous results of not seeking Jehovah have been briefly but powerfully sketched from the nation's past history and the conclusion is that they are not to fall away like their forefathers, the work for which there is a reward being the rooting out of idolatry. Delitzsch refuses all three tenses and argues the grammar, holding that the words must be taken generally with neither preterite nor future supplied but the first clause put in the present, and that many days is not an accusative of time, against the editor he answers, but the subject of the sentence; he then allows the whole historical range, from the defection after Joshua to the Assyrian and Babylonian exile and the present dispersion among all nations, on the authority of the threat Hosea utters with manifest reference to this verse.

Gill canvasses the Targum for the days of Jeroboam, the future reading fulfilled in the Babylonish captivity, and a Jewish reading by which the prophet foretold days when judgment should not be done in the world and the high priesthood and the sanhedrim should cease.

Clarke reports the same diversity of opinion and does choose, judging the reference to the people under Rehoboam and Abijah, happily changed under Asa, the most natural sense, against those who make it a prophecy of the final destruction of the Jews as a political existence. On the promise he turns polemical, holding that the unconditional perseverance of the saints has no place in this verse, being a doctrine which was first the ruin of the human race in the words ye shall not die and has ever since been the plague and disgrace of the Church; and he quotes the Targum, which he calls curious, for its paraphrase that the Word of the Lord shall be your helper while you walk in his ways and that if you cast away his fear he will abandon you.

Henry sets out three readings of the prophet's description without choosing between them: that it looks back as far as the days of the Judges, when they had priests but no teaching priests and elders but no law to any purpose; that it describes the ten tribes in Asa's own day, since Jeroboam's pretence of honouring the God who brought them out of Egypt had ended in downright infidelity, and no wonder when his priests were not teachers, for it is next to impossible that any religion should be kept up without a preaching ministry; or that the whole passage should be read in the future tense. On the conditional promise he finds both comfort and caution, that those who keep close to God shall always have his presence but no longer than they keep close.

debates: What period the prophet describes when he says Israel has been without the true God, where Henry lays out three readings and declines to choose, Clarke prefers the reigns of Rehoboam and Abijah, Ellicott takes it as past and illustrative, Gill canvasses the Targum and a future fulfilment in the captivity, and Delitzsch refuses the question of tense altogether.

Whether many days is an accusative of time or the subject of the sentence, which Delitzsch argues against the editor he answers, holding that the preposition expresses not being in a condition but coming into it.
Whether the conditional form of the promise bears on perseverance, which Clarke presses hard against the unconditional doctrine while Henry reads the same clause as comfort and caution together.
outliers: Henry observes that Israel was strangely addicted to idolatry while it had prophets, yet was pure from idolatry once prophecy had ceased and the canon was read in the synagogues, since the church could not be so easily imposed upon by a counterfeit Bible as by a counterfeit prophet.
Clarke asks whether our Lord alludes to these verses in his own discourse on wars and rumours of wars.

8.pericope_label: And when Asa heard these words, and the prophecy of Oded the prophet, he took courage, and put away the abominable idols out of all the land of Judah and Benjamin, and out of the cities which he had taken from mount Ephraim, and renewed the altar of the Lord, that was before the porch of the Lord. And he gathered all Judah and Benjamin, and the strangers with them out of Ephraim and Manasseh, and out of Simeon: for they fell to him out of Israel in abundance, when they saw that the Lord his God was with him. So they gathered themselves together at Jerusalem in the third month, in the fifteenth year of the reign of Asa. And they offered unto the Lord the same time, of the spoil which they had brought, seven hundred oxen and seven thousand sheep. And they entered into a covenant to seek the Lord God of their fathers with all their heart and with all their soul; That whosoever would not seek the Lord God of Israel should be put to death, whether small or great, whether man or woman. And they sware unto the Lord with a loud voice, and with shouting, and with trumpets, and with cornets. And all Judah rejoiced at the oath: for they had sworn with all their heart, and sought him with their whole desire; and he was found of them: and the Lord gave them rest round about.

schools.summary: Ellicott treats the corrupt name as the chapter's first problem, since the Hebrew gives the prophecy and then Oded the prophet without any connection, which is suspicious and suggests a marginal gloss that has crept into the text, especially as the opening verse names Azariah son of Oded; he proposes instead a gap in the text and notes that the Hebrew manuscripts show no variation while the versions only prove the difficulty ancient. He takes the renewal of the altar as reconsecration, the context implying it had been defiled by an illegal worship, while allowing the word may only mean repaired; handles the cities taken from the hill country of Ephraim, where the reference is generally thought inaccurate and to belong to Abijah's conquests, though Asa may have annexed border towns without resistance, Thenius having him assume the offensive after Baasha's retreat from Ramah; and works at the puzzle of Simeon, whose territory lay within the inheritance of Judah; he also supplies the calendar and legal frame of the covenant, the appointed day falling in Sivan, the oath binding the parties, the death clause a sanction prescribed by the law of Deuteronomy, and the closing clause meaning that God was at hand to them rather than found of them.

Gill reaches a conclusion on the name without the apparatus, mentioning the suggestion that a prophecy of the father was also delivered though not recorded, but preferring to identify Oded here with the son of Oded, as the Vulgate and Syriac and one Greek copy already do; on the covenant he adds the detail from Piscator that the parties passed between the pieces of a calf cut asunder.

Clarke suggests that the renewal of the altar was an enlargement, so that more sacrifices might be offered than before, since it cannot be supposed an altar had no victims on it until the fifteenth year of a king already zealous for restoring worship; he gives the incomers their motive, that men who had reflected on the promise to the house of David and found Jeroboam's government founded in idolatry would naturally leave their own country through a spirit of piety to go where they might worship the true God; and he sets out the covenant in two parts, to seek the God of their fathers with all the heart and to put to death any who would not, so that no toleration was given to idolatry.

Henry reads the altar's disrepair devotionally, that it was not above thirty-five years since Solomon's head was laid and yet ceremonial institutions wax old so soon, as things which in the fulness of time must vanish away; and he notices the reciprocity of the gathering, that the strangers came because they saw the Lord was with Asa, that his notice of them encouraged them in turn, and that although he ordered their gathering the text says they gathered themselves, making it their own act.

debates: How the corrupt name of the prophet in verse eight should be repaired, where Ellicott suspects a marginal gloss and proposes a gap in the text while Gill simply identifies Oded with the son of Oded, as three of the versions already do.

What the renewal of the altar means, which Ellicott takes as reconsecration after defilement by an illegal worship, Clarke as an enlargement to carry more sacrifices, and Henry as plain repair after thirty-five years.

Why Simeon appears among the incomers when its territory lay within the inheritance of Judah, where Ellicott offers a northward migration and a partial return, or religious isolation through the illegal worship at Beersheba, while granting that the second hardly agrees with the clause that they fell to him out of Israel.
outliers: Ellicott notes that the altar had now stood sixty years, and that the context of its renewal seems to imply reconsecration, the Greek and Latin both rendering the word dedicated.
Clarke holds that the oath confirming the covenant made it properly binding, and that God accepted them and their services.

16.pericope_label: And also concerning Maachah the mother of Asa the king, he removed her from being queen, because she had made an idol in a grove: and Asa cut down her idol, and stamped it, and burnt it at the brook Kidron. But the high places were not taken away out of Israel: nevertheless the heart of Asa was perfect all his days. And he brought into the house of God the things that his father had dedicated, and that he himself had dedicated, silver, and gold, and vessels. And there was no more war unto the five and thirtieth year of the reign of Asa.

schools.summary: Ellicott establishes that mother means grandmother and dismisses the theory that the mother of Abijah and the so-called mother of Asa were different women, one a daughter of Absalom and the other of Uriel of Gibeah, finding really no grounds for it. On the idol he does the close work: the word rendered idol means a thing of fear or a horror and is found only here and in the parallel, the phrase translated in a grove should rather be for Asherah, and the stamping, better rendered crushing, is the chronicler's own detail. He prefers a fresh explanation of the high-places discrepancy, that the earlier passage relates what the good king resolved and attempted while this one records his want of success, owing to the obstinate attachment of his people to their old sanctuaries. On the closing date he holds that the chronicler evidently modified the older text, which says war continued all their days, in order to date the outbreak precisely, and relays the solution of Thenius, that a letter standing for thirty entered the text by a doubled stroke so that the original readings were the fifth and sixth years, adding that the false dates probably existed already in the chronicler's source.

Gill limits the closing claim instead of repairing it, taking the verse to mean only that there was no further war with a foreign enemy, since animosities and hostilities of some sort continued with Baasha as long as he lived.

Clarke reports the Jewish tradition that the queen-mother repented and her name was changed to Michaiah daughter of Uriel, so that no mention of the former name should reproach her; he divides the high-places difficulty by holding that Asa totally suppressed the idolatry but permitted some of the places or altars to remain; and on the date he reports Ussher's view that the reckoning runs from the separation of the kingdoms and so falls in Asa's fifteenth year, suggests reading the five and twentieth instead, and then enters the chapter's most candid remark, that to settle these chronologies is a most difficult undertaking, that the difficulty does not belong to the sacred books alone since all other chronological tables of all the nations of the world are in the same predicament, and that he had often been puzzled by those of his own country even with access to all its archives.

Henry calls the deposing of the queen-mother bravely done of Asa, who would not connive at idolatry in those nearest him, knew he must honour God more than his grandmother, and dared not leave an idol in an apartment of his palace while destroying idols in the cities of his kingdom; he supposes she may have subscribed the association and so escaped the death the covenant decreed, though Asa still stripped her of her dignity and probably confined her to privacy. On the unremoved high places he offers his own division, that those in Judah's cities went but not those in the recovered cities of Israel, or that those for false gods went but not those used in the service of the God of Israel, and draws from it the moral that there may be defects in particular duties where the heart is still upright, since sincerity is something less than sinless perfection.

debates: How the thirty-fifth year is to be reconciled with the data of Kings, which produces three incompatible repairs: Thenius via Ellicott emends to the fifth and sixth years on a doubled letter, Clarke reports Ussher on counting from the separation and himself suggests the twenty-fifth, and Gill leaves the number alone and narrows what the verse claims.

Why the high places remained after a reformation the chapter calls thorough, where Ellicott distinguishes what Asa resolved from what he achieved against popular attachment, Clarke distinguishes the idolatry from its buildings, and Henry distinguishes Judah from the recovered cities and false worship from irregular worship of the true God.

Whether the Maachah deposed by Asa is the same woman as the mother of Abijah, which Ellicott affirms against the view that they were a daughter of Absalom and a daughter of Uriel respectively, while Clarke reports a tradition that she repented and was renamed.
outliers: Henry draws from the unfinished reformation that sincerity is something less than sinless perfection, there being defects in particular duties where the heart is nonetheless upright.
Ellicott compares the crushing of the idol with the treatment of the golden calf and of the high place at Bethel, and notes that the detail is added by the chronicler.
